A dashboard is a page of cards somebody built. Gauges, trends, lists of
entities, a button that starts the pump, a floor plan with the temperatures
sitting where the zones are. Build as many as the plant needs, give each to the
roles that need it or to the one screen it lives on, and the old Board is just
one of them.

It is in HotLoop IoT, Edge and Gateway. The Edge Relay has no UI and no
dashboards. The Edge HMI is built out of this page and nothing else, which is
the reason the rest of it is the way it is.

## Why it is built this way

**A card commands nothing.** The first design question for any page of buttons
is whether the page is a second way to run the plant. It isn't. A card names a
tag, an entity, a script or a recipe, and the browser does what every other
screen does with them. A write button posts to `POST /api/write`. An entity's
controls call `POST /api/services`. A script button opens the Scripts screen's
run prompt and a recipe card opens the Recipes screen's apply drawer. Every one
of those has its own permission and meets the write gate, so a dashboard can't
be a way round either. What `dashboards.write` guards is who decides what the
buttons are, which is an engineer's call and is admin-only for the same reason
writing a script is.

The consequence: a dashboard saved by an admin does nothing until an operator
presses something, and what the press does is exactly what pressing it on any
other screen does, down to the audit row.

**A layout is a flow, not coordinates.** Cards go in reading order. Each says
how wide it is out of twelve columns and how tall in rows, and knows nothing
about where it lands. Twelve columns on a panel PC, six on a laptop with another
window beside it, two on a tablet, one on a phone. A layout of pixel positions
is right on exactly the screen it was drawn on, and the Edge HMI has to be right
on whichever screen the machine has.

The consequence: nobody ever builds the phone version. There isn't one.

**Saves name the version.** Two people editing one dashboard is a thing that
happens at shift change. A save carries the `version` it was opened at, and a
stale one is refused with a `409` that says who got there first. Without that
the second person to press Save deletes the first one's afternoon without
either of them seeing it.

## The model

```json
{
  "id": "line-2",
  "name": "Line 2",
  "description": "The extruder, for the floor.",
  "kind": "cards",
  "roles": ["operator", "admin"],
  "homeFor": ["operator"],
  "screens": ["line-2-panel"],
  "position": 1,
  "version": 3,
  "cards": [
    {"id": "temp", "type": "gauge", "title": "Zone 1", "w": 3, "h": 3,
     "config": {"tag": "press-01/Zone1_Temp"}},
    {"id": "go", "type": "button", "w": 3, "h": 1,
     "config": {"tag": "line-02/Speed", "value": 250, "label": "Run at 250", "confirm": true}}
  ]
}
```

- **`id`** is lowercase letters, digits, hyphens and underscores, starting with
  a letter. It is in the address and never changes. `wall` is the wall board's.
- **`kind`** is `cards`, or `wall` for the wall board.
- **`roles`** are the roles offered the dashboard. Empty is every role. Whoever
  holds `dashboards.write` sees every dashboard whatever it says, because they
  have to be able to fix the one nobody else can open. A role that isn't offered
  one gets a `404` for it by name, so the list of what exists isn't something a
  viewer can learn by asking.
- **`homeFor`** are the roles it opens for when they come in with no address
  asking for anything. A role has at most one; the dashboard has to be offered
  to the roles it is home for.
- **`screens`** are the physical screens it is for. A screen name belongs to one
  dashboard.
- **`position`** orders the switcher. New ones go last.
- **`cards`** are in reading order, up to 60 per dashboard, 2 MB for all of
  them.
- **`version`** goes up by one on every save.

A card is `id` (unique in its dashboard, made by the page), `type`, an optional
`title`, `w` (1 to 12) and `h` (1 to 8), and a `config` that depends on the
type. Leave `w` and `h` out and the type's default is used. A config is checked
strictly: a key the type doesn't have is an error, and what is stored has every
default filled in. A card that names a tag, entity, script or recipe that
doesn't exist is refused when the dashboard is saved. A button on a tag that
isn't marked writable, or a button whose number is outside the tag's range, is
refused too: the gate would refuse every press, and the person building it
should hear that and not the person pressing it.

## The cards

| Type | What it is | Config | Default size |
|---|---|---|---|
| `status` | Devices up, tags reporting, alarms, historian, uptime: the Board's strip | none | 12 x 1 |
| `gauge` | One tag as the Board's dial, with its range and its alarm limits marked | `tag` | 3 x 3 |
| `value` | One tag as a big number, colored by its alarm state | `tag`, `decimals` | 3 x 2 |
| `trend` | Up to six tags over 15 minutes to a week | `tags`, `minutes`, `labels` | 6 x 3 |
| `entities` | The entities you pick, as their own tiles with their own controls | `entities` (up to 30) | 6 x 3 |
| `alarms` | The alarm list, with Acknowledge for whoever may | `outstanding`, `limit`, `devices`, `equipment` | 6 x 3 |
| `button` | Writes one value to one tag, after asking | `tag`, `value`, `label`, `confirm` | 3 x 1 |
| `script` | Runs a script through the Scripts screen's prompt | `script`, `label` | 3 x 1 |
| `recipe` | Picks one of up to eight recipes and opens its apply drawer | `recipes` | 4 x 2 |
| `markdown` | Text: headings, lists, bold, italic, code, http(s) links | `text` | 4 x 2 |
| `camera` | A snapshot that refreshes, or a motion JPEG stream | `url`, `stream`, `refreshSec` | 6 x 4 |
| `map` | A floor plan with live tags placed on it | `image`, `markers` | 6 x 5 |

Things worth knowing about the ones that aren't obvious:

- **`button`** sends `value` as the type it was saved as. A number is a number,
  `true` is a boolean, a string is text. `1` and `1.0` are different writes on a
  PLC and the gate decides by the JSON type, so the card doesn't turn one into
  the other. `confirm` is on unless it's switched off, and then it asks "this
  commands real equipment" with the current value and a reason that goes in the
  audit trail (`dashboard <id> / <card>` if left empty). Switching it off is for
  a panel where holding the button is the point; it is an engineer's decision and
  the Settings screen's "Confirm before writing" overrides it back on.
- **`alarms`** lists the whole plant's alarms unless you point it somewhere.
  `devices` is a list of device ids. `equipment` is a list of equipment node ids
  from `GET /api/equipment`, any level (a site, an area, a line, a cell), and a
  node stands for every device placed at or under it, so an area's page can show
  the area's alarms and nobody else's. With both, an alarm is listed when it is on
  either one. Leave them out, or empty, and the card is the whole plant, which is
  what every card saved before these fields did. The limit counts what is left
  after the filter, and `outstanding` still drops what is back to normal and
  acknowledged. A card limited to a place with no alarms says "here" so nobody
  reads it as a quiet plant, and a card whose equipment has since been deleted
  says that instead of showing an empty list. Equipment is stored as the node's
  id, so renaming or moving a node doesn't break the card. The dashboard is
  refused at save if a device or a node isn't there. In the builder you type the
  path (`Plant 2 / Scrubbers / Kettle 3`) and it keeps the id. This card reads
  the tree, so a role needs `equipment.read` (operators and viewers have it).

  ```json
  {
    "id": "kettle-alarms", "type": "alarms", "title": "Scrubber alarms", "w": 6, "h": 3,
    "config": { "outstanding": true, "limit": 10, "equipment": [14], "devices": ["oven-1"] }
  }
  ```
- **`trend`** draws the window you asked for, ending now, and not just the span
  the readings happened to cover: `minutes: 480` is an axis of the last eight
  hours with a tick on each round hour, in the time zone of whoever is looking.
  A tag that hasn't moved is a flat line at its last good reading, because that
  is what a stopped mill or a closed valve looks like, and the historian only
  keeps a reading when a value moves past its deadband, so there may be one
  reading in the window, or none. Nothing on the line is made up. What the tag
  held when the window began is its last good reading before it (`GET
  /api/history` says so with `carry=true`), and the line is that value from the
  start of the window to the first reading inside it. After the last reading it
  is held on to the last time the tag was heard from, never past now. There is no
  line before the first reading anybody has, and a tag whose last reading before
  the window was bad has no carry at all, because what it held is not known. A
  stretch of bad readings is a gap, the same as it always was. One reading on its
  own is a line to now, or a dot if there is nowhere to draw it to.

  The legend names each line by the tag's own name, the same name the number
  card shows, without the device in front. Two lines with the same name from
  different devices keep their full ids so you can tell them apart. `labels` is
  an optional object from a tag in `tags` to the text you want instead, 1 to 80
  characters, and a label for a tag that isn't plotted is refused. The hover
  tooltip always has the full id next to the label.

  ```json
  {
    "id": "mills", "type": "trend", "title": "Mill temperatures", "w": 6, "h": 3,
    "config": {
      "tags": ["plant-5-temperatures/Large Sand Mill Temperature", "plant-5-temperatures/Small Sand Mill Temperature"],
      "minutes": 480,
      "labels": { "plant-5-temperatures/Large Sand Mill Temperature": "Large mill" }
    }
  }
  ```
- **`camera`** loads the address in the browser, not on the server. A card's
  config is readable by every role that opens the dashboard, so an address with a
  login or a token in it is refused when the dashboard is saved. Use an address
  on the plant network that needs none, or a proxy that adds the login. A still
  is fetched again every `refreshSec` seconds with a `_hl` query parameter so the
  browser doesn't show the first one forever.
- **`map`** is a picture and markers. The picture is an http(s) address or one
  uploaded into the card (png, jpeg, webp or gif, up to 500 KB, stored in the
  card). Markers are tags, placed in percent of the picture's width and height so
  they stay where they were put at any size. This is a floor plan, not a street
  map: a tile map needs a tile server on the internet, and a plant's panel PC
  usually can't reach one.
- **`markdown`** is built into DOM nodes and never into HTML, so nothing typed
  into it can become markup or a script.
- **`gauge`, `value`, `map`** show "not on this gateway any more" if their tag
  is deleted after the dashboard was saved, instead of a dial that never moves.

## The wall board

The wall board is dashboard `wall`, kind `wall`. It is always there, it can't be
deleted, and it has no cards: its gauges are the tags pinned on the Board
screen, kept in the board's own setting where they always were. `GET` and `PUT
/api/board`, the `#board` address, the pin picker and the drag to arrange are
untouched.

What it gets from being a dashboard is the switcher (it is the first pill on
every dashboard and the Board has the bar too) and the assignments: it can be
offered to some roles, be a role's home, and be a physical screen's. A TV on the
wall opens `/?screen=wall-tv` and gets the Board with the header and tabs gone.

## Roles and screens

**Per role.** `roles` decides who is offered a dashboard. `homeFor` decides where
a role lands. An operator whose home is `line-2` opens HotLoop on Line 2. With a
URL fragment in the address (`#alarms`) the page opens where the address says.

**Per screen.** A screen is a physical display. Open HotLoop at
`/?screen=<name>` and it shows the dashboard whose `screens` has that name with
no header, no tabs and bigger touch targets, because nobody walking past a panel
PC has a use for a way out of the page. A name that no dashboard has says so
instead of showing something else.

**A panel signs people in, not itself.** With nobody signed in it shows a single
"PIN or badge" field. An operator types their PIN, or scans their badge (a
keyboard-wedge reader types it into the field), and the panel opens the
dashboard. Their name and a **Sign out** button sit in the corner, since the
header that would show them is gone. Every write a button on that dashboard makes
goes through the write gate as that person, and the audit trail and the Logbook
name them: "olga wrote 250 to line-02/Speed", not "panel-3". After fifteen minutes
of nobody touching the screen (a setting) the panel signs them out and goes back
to the field, and a write sent after that is refused. An admin gives each person
a code under **Settings, Users**. The whole of it, what a badge is, how the code
is stored and what it does not do, is in
[AUTH.md](/iot/authentication/#kiosk-panels-pin-or-badge-and-an-idle-sign-out).

On your own computer none of this applies: you are signed in with your password,
a button's write goes straight through the gate and logs you, and there is no
idle sign-out. A panel that was signed in with a standing operator account, the
way a panel had to be run before PINs, still works and still writes as that
account. Give a shared panel no such login.

This is what the Edge HMI is: a dashboard with `screens` set, on a machine that
opens that address, with the people at it signing in by PIN or badge.

## Building

Whoever holds `dashboards.write` (admins) sees **Edit** on a dashboard and
**New dashboard** in the bar. While editing:

- cards are inert, so grabbing a button to move it can't press it;
- drag a card onto another to put it there, or use the arrows on its toolbar,
  which are what a phone has, because a touchscreen doesn't start a drag;
- drag the corner to resize: the width snaps to a column of twelve, the height to
  a row;
- the gear edits the card, the copy button duplicates it, the cross deletes it;
- **Settings** is the name, who it is offered to, who it opens first for, its
  physical screens and its place in the switcher.

Nothing is saved until **Save**. **Discard** throws the changes away. A `409` on
save means somebody saved first: the page offers to load theirs.

## Layout

| Width | Columns | A card of `w` takes |
|---|---|---|
| Over 1100 px | 12 | `w` |
| 700 to 1100 px | 6 | half of `w`, rounded up |
| 480 to 700 px | 2 | one, or both when `w` is over 4 |
| Under 480 px | 1 | all of it |

Rows are 76 px with a 16 px gap on the wide layouts. On a phone a card is as tall
as its content with a floor from its rows, so nothing is cut off. The switcher
scrolls sideways inside itself and the page never does.

## On a phone

The web UI installs on a phone and opens with no connection. It's the same page
with a manifest, icons and a service worker, served by HotLoop itself, so there
is nothing to build and nothing to install on the server.

**Installing it.** On Android, Chrome's menu has **Install app**. On an iPhone,
Safari's Share sheet has **Add to Home Screen**. It opens full screen, with the
plant's name, and on Android a long press on its icon offers Alarms and Dashboards. A browser
only installs a page and runs a service worker over **https**, or on `localhost`.
On a plant's plain `http://` address HotLoop still opens in a tab exactly as it
always has, but it can't be installed and it won't work offline. Put a
certificate in front of it for phones (the ingress or the reverse proxy you
already have). The browser tells you why when it won't install: Chrome's
developer tools, Application, Manifest.

**What it keeps.** The page itself, and the last answer to the reads a person
looks at: the alarm list, the dashboards, the readings and entity states, the
devices and tags, the status, the equipment tree and the board. While the page is
open and connected it asks for those once a minute so there is something to open
to, and not while the phone is in a pocket. Open it with no connection and the
page loads, the alarm list and the dashboards show what the phone last saw, and a
bar across the bottom says so, with the time:

```
Offline. This is what this phone last saw as of 10/22/2026, 05:42:23. Nothing you
do here is sent until the connection is back.
```

When the connection is back, within a few seconds, the bar goes, the screen
refreshes from live answers and the live feed reconnects.

**What it never does.** Nothing that changes anything is sent from an offline
page. A write, whether it's a value to a tag, a script, a recipe or an
acknowledgement, is refused before it leaves the page, with the reason:

```
You are offline, so nothing was sent. Everything here is as of 10/22/2026, 05:42:23.
Try again when the connection is back.
```

The service worker doesn't answer, keep or queue a write, and there is no
background sync in it. A command to equipment is only ever sent by a person looking
at a live answer, and a button pressed with no connection is not waiting
somewhere to go out later. Acknowledging from a notification is a separate thing
and needs the network the same way: the ntfy app presses its own button.

**What it doesn't keep.** The live feed, trends and history, the logbook, the
settings, the users, the escalation policy and anything about notifications. Some
are too big and different every time to be worth keeping, and some hold things
(people's ntfy topics, accounts) that don't belong in a phone's cache, so those
screens need HotLoop to answer.

**On the phone.** What's kept lives in the browser's cache storage on that phone, at
most 200 answers, oldest dropped first. **Signing out empties it**, and so does a
session that has expired or been revoked (the first `401` empties it). Only a
signed-in session is ever kept, so an offline phone never opens to somebody else's
data. A new HotLoop version gets a page cache of its own and the old one is
deleted; the page is fetched live whenever there's a connection, so a new version
or a renamed plant shows on the next open.

**Where it's tested.** Chrome itself is asked whether the manifest parses and the
page is installable (`TestBrowserPhoneAppInstallsAndWorksOffline`: no manifest
errors, no installability errors, icons that are real PNGs of the size the
manifest says). The same test takes the server away, for the page and the worker
alike, and reloads: the page opens, the alarm list and a dashboard show what was
kept, a write to a tag and an Acknowledge are both refused, the alarm is still
unacknowledged and the write audit empty after the connection comes back, and
signing out empties what was kept. `TestServiceWorkerNeverTouchesAWrite` holds
the worker's source to the rule above. **Not verified**: installing on a real
phone, Safari on an iPhone (it reads the same tags, but nobody has run it), and a
real plant's Wi-Fi dropping out.

## Permissions

| Permission | Viewer | Operator | Admin |
|---|---|---|---|
| `dashboards.read` | yes | yes | yes |
| `dashboards.write` | no | no | yes |

Reading is every role's, filtered by `roles`. Writing is the admin's. What a card
can do when pressed is the pressing person's own permissions: a viewer sees a
write button disabled, and the server would refuse it if they got past that.

## The API

| Method | Route | Permission |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/api/dashboards` | `dashboards.read` |
| `POST` | `/api/dashboards` | `dashboards.write` |
| `GET` | `/api/dashboards/{id}` | `dashboards.read` |
| `PUT` | `/api/dashboards/{id}` | `dashboards.write` |
| `DELETE` | `/api/dashboards/{id}` | `dashboards.write` |

The reference with bodies and errors is in [API.md](/iot/api/#dashboards). Every
create, save and delete is on the record as a `config` event on subject
`dashboard:<id>`, so the Logbook says who changed what a panel shows.

The table is `dashboards`, added in migration 0023 for PostgreSQL, TimescaleDB
and SQLite. It only adds ([MIGRATIONS.md](/iot/migrations/)). The wall board's row is
made by the application when it is first asked for, not by the migration, so a
database restored from a backup taken before dashboards has it again.

## What isn't here

- **Pixel-exact layouts.** On purpose, above. If a machine's HMI really needs a
  control at a fixed spot, that is a screen built for that machine, and it is not
  what this is.
- **Per-card visibility.** A dashboard is offered to roles; a card isn't. Two
  audiences with different cards are two dashboards.
- **A tile map.** See the `map` card.
- **Holding a button.** A button writes once when pressed. A momentary control
  that writes on press and again on release is a different card and isn't built.
- **Dashboards in the Edge Relay.** It has no UI.
